catalog_quote: 2.7.3 Stress. The stress pattern of the prosodic word follows a trochaic pattern. Primary stress falls on the first syllable of the prosodic word as shown in examples (4)-(6) below. I have indicated the stressed syllable in bold letters. ... (4) be.na 'cow' (5) th'a.yi 'I play' (6) ne.du 'this' (7) kang.the 'conversation' (8) khaxh.cu 'from' When there is a closed syllable in a multisyllabic word, primary stress falls on the closed syllable. This is shown in examples (9)-(13) below; the stressed syllable is in bold. In these examples, the primary stress of each word is on the second syllable, which is CVC. Because CVC syllables draw stress, I infer that these syllables are heavy. Heavy CVC syllables without a vowel length distinction is typologically marked. (9) 7i.dung 'there' (10) kha.wel a wild green vegetable (11) ho.mang 'darkness' (12) di.phan 'over here' (13) wu.lang 'how much'

tone_statements.citation: Krishan, Shree (2001). A Sketch of Darma Grammar. In New Research on Zhangzhung and Related Himalayan Languages. Osaka: National Museum of Ethnology. pp. 347-400.
tone_statements.quote: Though Darma has three lexical tones, i.e. rising /á/, falling /à/, and level tone (unmarked), we have not been able to find them contrasting in many lexical items. It appears that due to the influence of Hindi and its dialects, in which these people have been bilingual for generations, the clear-cut distinctions in the tonal system have been considerably affected, giving rise to many homophonous words. ... Rising tone: /lá/ 'moon' /ká/ 'crow' /phú/ 'wild animal' ... Falling tone: /là/ 'rock' /kà/ 'excreta' /phù/ 'cow' ... Level tone: /la/ 'hand' /ro/ 'bone' /phu/ 'copper' Since the contrast in tone is restricted to only a few lexical items, it is left unmarked in the data.
tone_statements.summary: Three lexical tones (rising /á/, falling /à/, level unmarked) posited; author says the contrast is restricted to a few lexical items (Hindi contact) and leaves tone unmarked in the rest of the data.

audit.reasoning: The deciding quotation, both exception footnotes and the vowel-length statement are all verbatim in the held Willis 2007 dissertation at the stated pages (pp.72-73, fn.19 p.140, ch.4 fn.5 p.153, sect. 2.7.1). Willis 2007 is a 597-pp fieldwork grammar and Glottolog's top description; the classification (trochaic/initial default, CVC attracts primary stress = weight-sensitive, left edge, listed exceptions) follows the source directly. The held secondary source (Krishan 2001) and the newly downloaded CIIL 2015 phonology note are silent on stress; web search found no phonology article or instrumental study of Darma prosody. The one real gap is the same author's 2019 Brill grammar (paywalled), which could refine wording but rests on the same corpus and analysis, so no reclassification is indicated.
